intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 6 units · functions to interest

Grade 12 later does sequences, stats, coordinate geometry and matrices. This year is graphs of functions, plus similar triangles and money maths. Every worked box: *Given → formula → algebra → check forbidden values*.

units.title: Business Mathematics
units.intro:
**Simple interest:** I = Prt (r as a decimal, t in years). Amount A = P + I = P(1+rt).

**Compound:** A = P(1 + r/n)^nt if compounded n times a year. Yearly: A=P(1+r)^t.

cards.title: 6.1.1 Simple interest
body: **Words:** the **principal** $P$ is the money borrowed or saved; the **rate** $r$ is the percent charged per year; the **time** $t$ is in years; the **interest** $I$ is the extra money; the **amount** $A$ is principal + interest.
$$I = Prt, \qquad A = P + I = P(1 + rt)$$
Write $r$ as a decimal ($5\% = 0.05$) and $t$ in years (9 months $= \frac{9}{12} = 0.75$ year).
**Example 6.1:** 3500 Nakfa at 5% for 3 years: $I = 3500 \times 0.05 \times 3 = 525$ Nakfa, so $A = 4025$ Nakfa.

cards.title: 6.1.2 Compound interest
body: With **compound interest** the interest of each year is added to the principal, and next year's interest is worked out on the bigger sum: "interest on interest".
**Where the formula comes from:** each year the money is multiplied by $(1 + r)$:
- end of year 1: $P(1 + r)$;
- end of year 2: $P(1 + r)(1 + r) = P(1 + r)^2$;
- end of year $t$: $$A = P(1 + r)^t, \qquad \text{compound interest} = A - P.$$
Banks pay interest on savings and charge a higher rate on loans; the difference is how a bank earns its income.

cards.title: Reading Example 6.2
body: Simple interest is always $1000 \times 0.06 = 60$. Compound interest is 6% of the **previous amount**: $1060 \times 0.06 = 63.60$, then $1123.60 \times 0.06 = 67.42$. Berhe (simple) gets **1180** Nakfa; Saliha (compound) gets **1191.02** Nakfa. The book's first table multiplies 1060 and 1123.60 by 0.06 although simple interest always uses the original 1000, and it says "the amount to be paid to Saliha is 1180" where it means Berhe. In the second table "= 06" should be "= 60" and "1123.06" should be "1123.60".

cards.title: Simple grows in a straight line, compound bends upward

steps.text: Simple: the same 100 Nakfa is added every year, so the graph is a **straight line**: $A = 1000(1 + 0.1t)$.
Compound: each year the amount is **multiplied** by 1.1, so the graph curves upward: $A = 1000(1.1)^t$.
After 12 years: simple 2200, compound $1000 \times 1.1^{12} \approx 3138$ Nakfa, about 938 more. The longer the time, the bigger the gap.

cards.title: Compounding more than once a year
body: If interest is added $n$ times a year, each period uses the rate $\frac{r}{n}$ and there are $nt$ periods: $$A = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}$$
**Example 6.4(1):** 2500 Nakfa at 8% quarterly for 5 years: rate per quarter $0.02$, periods $20$: $A = 2500(1.02)^{20} = 3714.87$ Nakfa.
More frequent compounding gives slightly more: 12% yearly multiplies by 1.12, but 12% monthly multiplies by $1.01^{12} \approx 1.1268$ (an **effective rate** of 12.68%).

cards.answer: Compound interest earns 36 Nfa more because year 2 also earns interest on year 1’s interest.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Find the compound interest on $$3000\text{ Nakfa}$$ for $$8\text{ years}$$ at $$10\%$$ per annum compounded annually.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Calculate the accumulated amount ($$A$$)**
Use the compound interest formula $$A = P(1 + r)^t$$, where $$P = 3000$$, $$r = 0.10$$, and $$t = 8$$:
$$A = 3000(1 + 0.10)^8 = 3000(1.1)^8$$
$$A = 3000(2.1435888) = 6430.766\text{ Nakfa}$$

**Step 2: Calculate the compound interest ($$\text{CI}$$)**
$$\text{CI} = A - P = 6430.766 - 3000 = 3430.766\text{ Nakfa}$$
Rounding to two decimal places yields $$3430.80\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Result:** **$$3430.80\text{ Nakfa}$$**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: An amount of $$6000\text{ Nakfa}$$ is borrowed for $$4\text{ years}$$ at simple interest. If the total interest paid is $$720\text{ Nakfa}$$, what is the annual interest rate?

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: An amount of $$6000\text{ Nakfa}$$ is borrowed for $$4\text{ years}$$ at simple interest. If the total interest paid is $$720\text{ Nakfa}$$, what is the annual interest rate?
cards.why:
**Step 1: State the simple interest formula**
The simple interest formula is:
$$I = Prt$$

**Step 2: Substitute the known values**
Here, $$I = 720$$, $$P = 6000$$, and $$t = 4$$:
$$720 = 6000 \times r \times 4$$
$$720 = 24000 \times r$$

**Step 3: Solve for $$r$$**
$$r = \frac{720}{24000} = 0.03$$
Converting to percentage:
$$\text{Rate} = 0.03 \times 100 = 3\%$$
**Result:** **$$3.0\%$$**.

cards.title: 6.1.3 Instalment plan
body: An **instalment plan** lets you take an item now and pay for it (price + interest) in a sequence of equal payments. Often there is a **down payment** (deposit) first.
**Total instalment cost** = down payment + (number of payments) × (each payment).
**Charge for credit** (the interest) = total instalment cost − cash price.
**Example 6.5(1):** TV 12,000 Nakfa; 2400 down and 48 payments of 230: total $2400 + 48 \times 230 = 13{,}440$; credit charge 1440 Nakfa.
**Example 6.5(2) (simple interest):** dress 2500, 10% deposit (250), balance 2250 at 7.5% for 2 years: $A = 2250(1 + 0.075 \times 2) = 2587.50$; monthly payment $2587.50 \div 24 = 107.81$ Nakfa.

cards.title: Example 6.5(3): equal yearly instalments with compound interest

steps.text: Helen owes 66,200 at 10%. Year 1: $66200 \times 1.1 = 72{,}820$; she pays $x = 26{,}620$, leaving 46,200.
Year 3: $24200 \times 1.1 = 26{,}620$; the last payment clears it exactly.

cards.title: Finding the equal instalment
body: Move every payment to the **end**: the first payment earns interest for 2 years, the second for 1, the last for 0. Together they must equal the loan grown for 3 years:
General rule (loan $P$, rate $r$ per period, $n$ payments): grow every payment to the end of the loan and set the total equal to $P(1 + r)^n$:
$$x\left[(1 + r)^{n-1} + \dots + 1\right] = P(1 + r)^n$$
(The book's check lists "10% of 33100", "10% of 3310", "10% of 1210" — it means 10% of 66,200, 46,200 and 24,200; the interest values printed are right.)

cards.title: 6.1.4 Depreciation
body: Machines, cars and buildings (**fixed assets**) lose value with age and use. The loss is the **depreciation**; the value left is the **book value** (BV).
$$\text{depreciation} = \text{original cost (OC)} - \text{book value (BV)}$$
**Straight-line method:** the same amount every year: $$\text{annual dep.} = \frac{OC - BV}{t}$$
$$\text{rate} = \frac{\text{annual dep.}}{OC} \times 100\%$$
$$BV = OC(1 - rt)$$
**Diminishing (reducing) value method:** the same **percent** of last year's value each year: $$BV = OC\left(1 - r\right)^t.$$ It is compound interest run backwards.

cards.title: How to fill a diminishing schedule
body: Each row: depreciation $= 40\% \times$ last book value; new book value $=$ last book value $-$ depreciation (or simply $\times 0.6$); accumulated $=$ last accumulated $+$ this year's depreciation. Check: accumulated $=$ 4800 $-$ book value. (The book prints the year-4 accumulated depreciation as 3177.92; it is 4177.92.)

steps.text: Straight line: 5100 → 900 by 840 every year — a straight line.
Reducing 30% a year: $5100 \times 0.7^t$ — big drops first, small later; after 5 years about 857.
Year 1 loss: 840 (straight line) vs 1530 (reducing). Cars really lose most value early, so the reducing method is more realistic for them.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Complete the depreciation schedule: A machine costs $$5100\text{ Nakfa}$$. Under straight-line method, annual depreciation is $$840\text{ Nakfa}$$. What is the book value at the end of Year 2?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Calculate total depreciation over 2 years**
Since straight-line depreciation is constant:
$$\text{Total Depreciation} = 2 \times 840 = 1680\text{ Nakfa}$$

**Step 2: Calculate the book value at Year 2**
$$\text{Book Value} = \text{Original Cost} - \text{Total Depreciation}$$
$$\text{Book Value} = 5100 - 1680 = 3420\text{ Nakfa}$$
**Result:** **$$3420\text{ Nakfa}$$**.

cards.title: 6.2 Partnership: four ways to share profit
body: A **partnership** is a business owned by two or more people who share management and profit. The money each puts in is the **capital** (investment).
1. **Equal shares:** profit $\div$ number of partners (Example 6.8(1): $99000 \div 3 = 33000$).
2. **Agreed ratio** $a : b$: one part $= \frac{\text{profit}}{a + b}$ (Example 6.8(2): 2 : 3 of 20,000 gives 8000 and 12,000).
3. **Ratio of capital** (Example 6.8(3)): each gets $\frac{\text{own capital}}{\text{total capital}} \times$ profit.
4. **Salary or interest first, then ratio** (Example 6.8(4)): take the salaries/interest out first and share only what is left.
If money stays in for different times, use **capital × time** as the share ratio.

cards.title: Example 6.8(3) as a bar
body: Belay 60,000 and Gilai 90,000: ratio $60 : 90 = 2 : 3$, so 5 equal parts of $70000 \div 5 = 14000$. Belay $2 \times 14000 = 28000$, Gilai $3 \times 14000 = 42000$.

cards.title: Worked example: salary first (Example 6.8(4))
cards.problem: Goitom (150,000) and Abdella (300,000) own a restaurant; the manager is paid 30,000 a year. Profit 90,000. Share it by investment.

cards.title: Partnership: sharing profit
body: Partners usually share profit (or loss) in the **ratio of their capital**. If the money is invested for different lengths of time, use capital × time.

cards.title: Worked example: sharing profit
cards.problem: (a) A invests 30,000 Nfa and B 20,000 Nfa; profit 15,000 Nfa. (b) A invests 20,000 Nfa for 12 months and B 30,000 Nfa for 6 months; profit 14,000 Nfa. Share each profit.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Three partners invest $$60,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, $$90,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, and $$150,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ respectively. If they divide a total profit of $$70,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ proportionally based on their investment, what is the share of the first partner?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Calculate total capital**
$$\text{Total Capital} = 60000 + 90000 + 150000 = 300000\text{ Nakfa}$$

**Step 2: Calculate the share of the first partner**
$$\text{Share} = 70000 \times \frac{60000}{300000} = 70000 \times \frac{1}{5} = 14000\text{ Nakfa}$$
**Result:** **$$14,000\text{ Nakfa}$$**.

cards.title: 6.2 Mixtures
body: A mixture problem asks how much of each ingredient to use. Two standard tools:

**1. A table with two equations.** One equation for the **total amount**, one for the **amount of the pure part** (percent × quantity). Example 6.9(1): $x + y = 100$ and $0.30x + 0.55y = 0.40 \times 100$ give $x = 60$ kg, $y = 40$ kg.
**2. Alligation (price mixtures):** to mix a cheap item (price $c$) and a dear item (price $d$) to get a mean price $m$: $$\text{cheap} : \text{dear} = (d - m) : (m - c).$$
**3. Keep the unchanged part fixed:** when you add only one ingredient, the other stays the same amount — work with that one (Example 6.9(4)).

steps.text: Write the two prices on the left and the mixture price 5 in the middle.
Subtract along the diagonals (always bigger minus smaller): $8 - 5 = 3$ and $5 - 3 = 2$.
Each difference lands opposite its own price: wheat gets 2 parts, sorghum 3 parts. **wheat : sorghum = 2 : 3.** Check: $\frac{2 \times 8 + 3 \times 3}{5} = 5$.

cards.title: Worked example: Example 6.9(2)
cards.problem: How many litres of a 20% solution must be added to 40 litres of an 80% solution to get a 50% mixture?

steps.text: Let $x$ litres of 20% be added. Pure part: $0.2x + 0.8 \times 40 = 0.2x + 32$.

cards.answer: 40 litres of the 20% solution (mixed with the 40 litres of the 80% solution — the book wrongly says "55%")

cards.title: Worked example: the part that does not change (Example 6.9(4))
cards.problem: 120 cm³ of soil-and-fertiliser is 10% fertiliser. How much fertiliser must be added to make it 28% fertiliser?

steps.text: In the new mixture soil is $100\% - 28\% = 72\%$: $0.72 \times \text{new total} = 108$.
New total $= 150$ cm³, so add $150 - 120 = 30$ cm³.

body: r=10% is 0.10 not 10. Months → t=m/12. “Discount 10% then tax 10%” is not back to the start (0.9×1.1=0.99).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A TV set with a cash price of $$12,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ is bought on installment plan. If the buyer makes a down payment of $$2400\text{ Nakfa}$$ and 48 monthly payments of $$230\text{ Nakfa}$$, what is the total cost of credit (finance charge)?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Calculate total installment payment**
$$\text{Total Payments} = \text{Down Payment} + (\text{Installment} \times \text{Periods})$$
$$\text{Total Payments} = 2400 + (230 \times 48) = 2400 + 11040 = 13440\text{ Nakfa}$$

**Step 2: Calculate the cost of credit**
$$\text{Finance Charge} = \text{Total Payments} - \text{Cash Price}$$
$$\text{Finance Charge} = 13440 - 12000 = 1440\text{ Nakfa}$$
**Result:** **$$1440\text{ Nakfa}$$**.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Simple: $I = Prt$, $A = P(1 + rt)$. Compound: $A = P(1 + \frac{r}{n})^{nt}$.
Instalments: total cost $-$ cash price $=$ credit charge; equal yearly payments: grow each payment to the end.
Depreciation: straight line $BV = OC(1 - rt)$; diminishing $BV = OC(1 - r)^t$.
Partnership: share in the agreed ratio (capital, capital × time), after salaries/interest.
Mixtures: conserve the pure part; alligation cheap : dear $= (d - m) : (m - c)$.

glossary.meaning: The money borrowed, lent or saved.
Interest worked out on the principal plus earlier interest.
Paying for an item with a deposit and a sequence of equal payments.
The loss in value of a fixed asset: original cost − book value.
The estimated value of an asset after some years.
A business owned by two or more people who share profits.
A quick rule for the ratio of two items mixed to a given mean price.

tips.text: Read 6.1 The Banking System again and say its main idea in one sentence.
Rate as a decimal, time in years.
Compound: multiply by (1 + r) each period.
Diminishing depreciation is compound interest with (1 − r).

questions.tip: Compound ≥ simple for $t \ge 1$.
questions.label: 6.1 Practice — simple and compound interest

questions.q: Exercise 6.3 Q1–Q2: number of periods and rate per period: (a) 4 years, 6%, half-yearly (b) 2 years, 8%, quarterly (c) 1.5 years, 12%, monthly. Also 8% per year as half-yearly, quarterly, monthly rates.
questions.tip: Divide the rate, multiply the time.

questions.q: Exercise 6.3 Q3–Q4: compound interest on (a) 4000 Nakfa, 1.5 years, 8% half-yearly; (b) 800 Nakfa, 1 year, 6% quarterly.
questions.tip: Rate per period and number of periods first.
questions.label: 6.1 Practice — simple and compound interest

questions.q: Exercise 6.3 Q5–Q7: (5) interest on 2500 Nakfa, 5 years, 4% half-yearly; (6) amount of 20,000 Nakfa, 8 years, 4% quarterly; (7) interest on 25,000 Nakfa, 12 years, 6% half-yearly.
questions.tip: Use the $x^y$ key.

questions.q: Review Q3: how much must be deposited now at 6% compound interest to have 8000 Nakfa in 5 years?

questions.q: Review Q4–Q5: (4) 3500 Nakfa compounded quarterly becomes 5735.16 in 5 years: interest? rate? (5) Population 4 million grows 2.5% a year: after 2 years?
questions.tip: Population growth = compound interest.
questions.label: 6.1 Practice — simple and compound interest

questions.q: How long does money take to double at 8% compounded yearly?
questions.tip: Rule of 72: $72 \div 8 = 9$.
questions.label: 6.1 Practice — simple and compound interest

questions.q: Which gives the most after 1 year on 1000 Nakfa at 12% per year?
why: Step 1: monthly $1000(1.01)^{12} = 1126.83$; half-yearly 1123.60; yearly and simple 1120.
questions.tip: More periods ⇒ more interest.
questions.label: 6.1 Practice — simple and compound interest

questions.q: With simple interest the interest in year 3 is bigger than in year 1.
why: Step 1: simple interest is $Pr$ every year, always on the original principal.
questions.tip: Only compound interest grows each year.
questions.label: 6.1 Practice — simple and compound interest

questions.q: Exercise 6.4 Q2: a cupboard costs 8500 Nakfa; on instalments over 3 years the price rises by 17.5%. (a) total (b) interest (c) yearly instalment.

questions.q: Exercise 6.4 Q3: a radio costs 8500 Nakfa; 1500 down and 48 payments of 184.34. Total and interest?

questions.q: Exercise 6.4 Q4: wheat worth 3750 Nakfa, nothing down, 12 payments of 330.16. Annual (simple) interest rate?

questions.tip: Rate is on the original cost.
questions.label: 6.1 Practice — instalments and depreciation

questions.q: Exercise 6.5 Q3: 20 computers at 40,000 each; BV 4000 each after 12 years (straight line). Annual depreciation and rate?

questions.q: With straight-line depreciation the book value falls by the same percent every year.
why: Step 1: it falls by the same **amount**; as the value shrinks that amount is a bigger percent.
questions.tip: Same amount = straight line; same percent = diminishing.

similar.q: Diminishing value falls by the same amount?

questions.label: 6.1 Practice — instalments and depreciation

questions.q: Exercise 6.6 Q3: profits/losses in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. (a) Share a profit of 9000. (b) How is a loss shared?
why: Step 2: losses follow the same agreed ratio.
questions.tip: Total parts $= 2 + 3 + 7$.
questions.label: 6.2 Practice — partnership and mixtures

questions.q: Exercise 6.6 Q4: Salem 60,000, Dawd 30,000; each takes 10% interest on capital, the rest is split equally. Profit 15,000.

questions.label: 6.2 Practice — partnership and mixtures

questions.q: Exercise 6.6 Q5: capitals 14,000, 17,000, 33,000. 10% of a 6000 profit goes to a national programme; the rest by capital.
questions.tip: Total parts first.
questions.label: 6.2 Practice — partnership and mixtures

questions.tip: Return first, then ratio.
questions.label: 6.2 Practice — partnership and mixtures

questions.q: Exercise 6.7 Q5: 90 litres of acid and water is 60% water. How much water to make it 75% water?

questions.label: 6.2 Practice — partnership and mixtures

questions.tip: The mean is closer to the item used more.
questions.label: 6.2 Practice — partnership and mixtures

questions.q: If partners invest different amounts for different times, the profit is shared in the ratio of capital × time.
why: Step 1: 1000 Nakfa for 2 months does the same work as 2000 for 1 month.
questions.tip: Multiply before comparing.
questions.label: 6.2 Practice — partnership and mixtures
